title: Two names, one list
summary: b = a does not copy a list: both names point at the same one. Copy it with [:], list() or copy(), and tell == from is.

intro.text:
A name does not hold a list. It **points at** one. So this line copies nothing:

```
backup = scores
```

Now two names point at **the same list**. Change the list through one name (`scores.append(90)`) and the other name sees it too, because there is only one list. With strings this never mattered, since a string can never be changed. With lists it matters a lot.

Two different things can happen to a name:

- **change the object** it points at (`append`, `xs[0] = ...`): every name on that object sees the change
- **move the name** to a new object (`xs = [...]`): only that one name moves

To get a separate list, **copy** it. All three of these do the same:

- `scores[:]` (a slice of everything)
- `list(scores)`
- `scores.copy()`

Two checks tell the cases apart. `==` asks: **same items?** `is` asks: **the very same object?** A copy is `==` but not `is`.

The **refs** panel draws every name as an arrow to its object. Two arrows into one box means one shared list.
intro.analogy: A shared online document. Sending a link (b = a) gives a second way into the same document, so an edit by either person shows up for both. Downloading a copy (a[:]) gives you your own file that nobody else's edits can touch.

predict.why: b = a made b point at the same list. append changed that one list, so b sees 3 too.

predict.q: What does this print? Type it exactly.
predict.why: x[:] made a separate copy. Only x got the new item, so x has 3 items and y still has 2.
Line 3 moves only the name p to a new list. q still points at the first list, which was never changed.
Two lists were made, with the same items. == compares the items (True), is asks whether they are one object (False).

today: ['bread', 'eggs', 'tea']
tomorrow: ['eggs', 'tea']

quiz.q: After `a = [1]`, `b = a` and `b.append(2)`, what is a?
quiz.why: a and b point at one list, so a change through b shows through a.

quiz.q: Which line makes ys a separate copy of xs?
quiz.why: A slice of everything is a new list. ys = xs only adds a second name.

options: Whether two names point at the very same object
Whether two lists have the same items
Whether a value is in a list
quiz.why: is checks identity. == checks the items.

quiz.q: After `a = [1]`, `b = a` and `a = [5]`, what is b?
quiz.why: a = [5] moves only the name a. b still points at the first list.

quiz.q: Why did sharing never cause surprises with strings?
options: A string can never be changed, so no change can show through another name
Two names cannot point at one string
Python forbids b = a for strings
quiz.why: Only objects that can change in place, like lists, show a change through a second name.

quiz.q: With `inner = [0]` and `outer = [inner, inner]`, what does `inner.append(1)` then `print(outer)` show?
quiz.why: Both items of outer point at the same inner list, so the change shows twice.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the brackets on copy
mistakes.explain: Without ( ) you store the copy method itself, not a copied list. Call it: first.copy().

mistakes.title: Emptying a list that is shared
mistakes.explain: done is not a second list, it is a second name for todo. Popping both items emptied the one list, so done has nothing at position 0.

mistakes.title: Calling copy on its own
mistakes.explain: There is no copy function to call on its own. Use the list method pets.copy(), or list(pets).
